hints: Start by separating the two bar types in Fig. 3.1 - grey for case incidence and white for mortality rate - and check for each country whether the bar goes up (+) or down (-) from zero.
Look for the odd-one-out for case incidence and the common pattern for mortality rate across all four countries.
Identify which country shows the longest downward grey bar and which shows the longest downward white bar to find the greatest reductions.
Pick out approximate percentage values from the y-axis to support each trend, for example about +60% or about -80 to -95%.
walkthrough:
Separate The Two Measures**
Think of case incidence as how many new cases occur and mortality rate as how many deaths occur. In Fig. 3.1 grey bars are incidence and white bars are mortality. A bar above zero means an increase from 2010 to 2015, a bar below zero means a decrease, which is good progress.

Describe Case Incidence**
Only Lao PDR has a grey bar above zero at about +60%, so it is the only country where new cases got worse. Cambodia, Solomon Islands and Papua New Guinea all have grey bars below zero. Papua New Guinea has the longest downward grey bar at about -82%, so it made the most progress on reducing new cases.

Describe Mortality Rate**
All four white bars are below zero, so every country reduced deaths. Lao PDR fell by about -92%, Cambodia by about -95%, Solomon Islands by about -66% and Papua New Guinea by about -76%. Cambodia has the longest downward white bar, so it shows the greatest reduction in mortality.

Final answer: Case incidence: only Lao PDR increased, by approx. +60%; all other countries decreased, with Papua New Guinea showing the greatest reduction of approx. 82%. Mortality rate: all four countries decreased, with Cambodia showing the greatest reduction of approx. 95%.

hints: Recall which organism transmits Plasmodium between people and when it normally feeds.
Think of the net in two ways - what the mesh itself does physically, and what the insecticide coating does chemically to the mosquito population.
walkthrough:
Link Mosquito Bites To Malaria Spread**
Malaria is not spread directly person to person. The female Anopheles mosquito is the vector - it takes a blood meal, picks up Plasmodium parasites and passes them on at the next bite. It feeds mainly at night when people are sleeping under nets.

Explain The Double Action Of ITNs**
The fine mesh acts as a physical barrier so mosquitoes cannot reach the sleeping person to feed. At the same time the insecticide coating kills mosquitoes on contact or reduces their numbers. Fewer bites and fewer vectors means the transmission cycle is broken, so both new cases and deaths fall.

Final answer: Nets provide a physical barrier preventing bites by female Anopheles mosquitoes, the vector, which feed mainly at night when people sleep. Insecticide kills or reduces numbers of mosquitoes, breaking the transmission cycle of Plasmodium.

hints: Compare Table 3.1 carefully - what different Plasmodium protein does each test stick have to detect?
Recall why any antibody only binds one antigen shape, thinking about the variable region and complementary binding site.
walkthrough:
Spot That The Targets Are Different**
From Table 3.1, stick 1 has to detect pLDH (parasite lactate dehydrogenase) while stick 2 has to detect HRP-2 (histidine-rich protein 2). These are different proteins with different amino acid sequences and therefore different 3D shapes.

Apply Antibody Specificity**
A monoclonal antibody binds only its complementary antigen because its variable region forms a specific binding site shape. The mobile antibody must first bind one part of the protein and then the immobilised antibody binds another part to trap it. So each stick needs a monoclonal antibody with a variable region complementary to its own target protein.

Final answer: Test stick 1 detects pLDH and test stick 2 detects HRP-2, different antigens. Antibodies are specific with different variable regions / antigen-binding sites complementary to each protein, so different mobile monoclonal antibodies are needed to bind each protein.

hints: Work out what a positive on stick 1 alone tells you, using the list of species that produce pLDH in Table 3.1.
Work out what a negative on stick 2 rules out, since HRP-2 is made by only one species.
walkthrough:
Interpret The Positive pLDH Result**
A coloured line in the test window means the protein was trapped between mobile and immobilised antibodies. Positive on stick 1 means pLDH is in the blood, so Plasmodium is present. Table 3.1 shows pLDH is made by all four species: P. vivax, P. falciparum, P. ovale and P. malariae.

Use The Negative HRP-2 Result To Narrow It Down**
Negative on stick 2 means no HRP-2 was trapped, so no coloured line forms. Table 3.1 shows HRP-2 is made by P. falciparum only. Together the results diagnose malaria caused by one of the non-falciparum species - P. vivax, P. ovale or P. malariae - and rule out P. falciparum.

Final answer: Positive stick 1 shows Plasmodium infection as pLDH present. Negative stick 2 shows no HRP-2 so no P. falciparum. Infection is with P. vivax, P. ovale or P. malariae, but not P. falciparum.
